text: of Duluth’s initial interest in the RACER grant was to vet and prioritize projects for implementation, as resilience is advanced through actual projects, not just project plans. Financial projections for projects assumed continued availability of federal tax credits and policies that made direct pay available to municipalities. Although the framework developed under F3 provides flexibility as policy environments change, current policy uncertainty and staffing turnover has created an uncertain timeframe for solar and storage buildouts as identified through this project. Aligned partnerships first explored under RACER may result in new City/utility partnerships. In the past, the City has worked to install solar that is owned and operated by Minnesota Power on vacant land owned by the City, but has not installed anything over 45kW with City infrastructure. Using permanent community infrastructure and assets to spur renewable energy development is something that not many communities have been able to do. While many other communities utilize small-scale rooftop solar, micro-solar PV on streetlights, and community solar run by third party development companies, it is a priority for the City of Duluth to incorporate large-scale solar into the fabric of the community. The proposed Bayview project will be pursued as a model for scaling additional solar developments that have been identified through RACER research. Developing this project gives the community and administration a baseline of what the actual solar costs and benefits are, both economically and socially, in order to institute solar on other identified sites. Additional sites that the City of Duluth plans to install solar on include two pump stations and reservoirs, the City owned water treatment plant, two firehalls, two police stations, three community centers, and the City owned natural gas utility. RACER has provided a baseline for cost, energy savings, and community benefits, and guides plans for these potential installations. Implementing projects in Duluth at this scale could save the city a potential $553,361 per year and transform the City’s operating budget approach. While not all identified sites have the opportunity to directly offset LMI household energy costs like the potential Bayview project, each site provides a certain community benefit, from resilience hubs and resources distribution to ensuring emergency services are efficient and affordable. Accomplishing implementation of these plans will be dependent of financial resources and available incentives. The advantage of completing both a top-down and bottom-up approach is that multiple community partners can be involved in advancing the community-based minimum resilience standards as potential City-based solar projects seek financing and administrative approval. The immediate next steps for building community resilience are driven by the community's ranked priorities, focusing primarily on individual action planning assisted by the Community Stakeholder Group and led community-based organization, Ecolibrium3. Informational outreach and development of partnerships to aid community members in building their own preparedness and resilience resources will be pursued with the assistance of Ecolibrium3’s AmeriCorps programs.
